newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council gives up on criticism of Iraqi attacks.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council gives up on criticism of Iraqi attacks.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council on Friday gave up trying to get a unified response to Iraq's incursion into the Kurdish north, reflecting an intense conflict between Russia and several Western nations.
Britain, which had sponsored a resolution criticising Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's government, decided not to continue the debate after Russia threatened to veto it.
"The council is not able to proceed on the draft resolution that the United Kingdom has put forward," Britain's Deputy Ambassador Stephen Gomersall said.

"Britain deeply regrets that the council is not in a position to adopt a resolution on Iraqi oppression of its people despite clear indications that the council would endorse such a resolution," he said. "We are concerned about reports that Iraq is still involved in operations and that executions are continuing apace."

U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright, who broke off a trip to South America because of the Iraqi crisis, said the situation "shows that sometimes the council is not the most effective way to deal with this."
"We stand by what the United States did to deal with the problem in the northern governates and it's just unfortunate that at this stage was council was not able to speak," she said.

The deadlock illustrated the crumbling of the coalition that backed Washington in the Gulf War, with the United States coming under increasing criticism for firing cruise missiles against Iraq and then claiming it had U.N. authorisation to do so. The U.S. intervention is the main reason the council could not agree on the wording of a text, diplomats said.

Britain had already softened some provisions to meet objections from France and other members but Russia blocked a vote. Russia, the United States, Britain, France and China have veto power in the 15-seat council, which needs nine votes and no veto to adopt any resolution.

In addition the lack of council action sends a signal to Saddam that the United States and Britain are fairly isolated in their views. China, Egypt and Indonesia also had objections but diplomats said none were as serious as those of Russia.

Russia argued that the resolution was an attempt to give legal underpinnings to U.S. military actions against Iraq by not mentioning any of the cruise missile attacks launched by Washington in response to Baghdad's incursion.
Russian Ambassador Sergei Lavrov told reporters "because the situation evolved in northern Iraq there is no need to demand from anybody to withdraw any troops or do anything."

Gomersall said Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali would decide when conditions were ripe for implementing the oil-for-food deal, which the U.N. chief put on hold last weekend after Iraqi troops moved into the north to fight one Kurdish faction allied to Iran.

Italy asked for the oil deal to receive further consideration in the council to make sure "it is kept in play," said the current council president, Alfredo Lopes Cabral of Guinea-Bissau. But Gomersall said the events this week would make it difficult for "Boutros-Ghali to go ahead."
The plan allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other supplies for its people suffering under six years of crippling U.N. trade sanctions.
